items.prompt_md: What does a queen at (r, c) block in the three conflict sets?
options: Column c, diagonal r - c, and anti-diagonal r + c
Only row r
Column c and row r
Diagonals r and c
items.answer: Column c, diagonal r - c, and anti-diagonal r + c
items.explanation_md: Along a down-right diagonal r - c is constant and along a down-left diagonal r + c is constant. Rows need no set because we place exactly one queen per row.

items.prompt_md: Why does the N-Queens search place one queen per row instead of choosing any n squares?
options: It makes diagonals impossible
It removes row conflicts by construction, cutting the search from choosing squares to just choosing a column per row
It is required by the output format
It guarantees that a solution exists
items.answer: It removes row conflicts by construction, cutting the search from choosing squares to just choosing a column per row
items.explanation_md: Two queens in a row would attack each other, so any valid board has exactly one per row. Iterating rows enforces that for free.

items.prompt_md: What is the purpose of the 'undo' step after recursing in constraint placement?
options: It deletes the solution from the output
It speeds up the next recursive call
It removes the placement from the conflict sets so the next candidate in the same row is checked against the correct state
It sorts the columns
items.answer: It removes the placement from the conflict sets so the next candidate in the same row is checked against the correct state
items.explanation_md: The sets must reflect only the queens currently on the board. Skipping the undo leaves phantom attacks that wrongly rule out valid squares.

items.prompt_md: For Sudoku, which three kinds of sets track conflicts, and how do you find the box of cell (r, c)?
options: Only row sets, with box = r + c
Column and diagonal sets, with box = r - c
One global set, with box = r * c
Row, column and 3x3 box sets, with the box index computed as (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3
items.answer: Row, column and 3x3 box sets, with the box index computed as (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3
items.explanation_md: A digit may appear only once in its row, its column and its 3x3 box. Integer division maps each cell to one of 9 boxes.

items.prompt_md: When is a partial placement pruned?
options: As soon as the candidate violates a rule, before recursing into any deeper rows
Only after all n queens are placed and validated
Only when the board is symmetric
Never; pruning changes the answer
items.answer: As soon as the candidate violates a rule, before recursing into any deeper rows
items.explanation_md: Checking before recursing means a bad prefix never spawns its subtree. Validating at the end would produce the same answers but explore n^n boards.

items.prompt_md: A student appends the shared `placed` list directly to the answer instead of building a board each time. What goes wrong?
options: The search runs out of memory
Every stored solution aliases the same list and is overwritten as the search continues
The solution count is too high
Nothing; lists are copied on append
items.answer: Every stored solution aliases the same list and is overwritten as the search continues
items.explanation_md: Python appends a reference. Because backtracking keeps mutating `placed`, the earlier answers change too. Build a fresh board (or copy) at the moment of recording.

items.prompt_md: What is the standard worst-case time bound for N-Queens with one queen per row?
options: O(n!), since row 0 has n options, row 1 at most n - 1 safe columns, and so on
O(n log n)
items.answer: O(n!), since row 0 has n options, row 1 at most n - 1 safe columns, and so on
items.explanation_md: Column conflicts alone leave at most n - i choices at row i, giving n! leaves. Diagonal pruning makes the real count much smaller, but the bound remains factorial.

items.prompt_md: What is the space complexity of the N-Queens search, excluding the output?
options: O(n^2) for the board
O(n!) for the tree
O(n): recursion depth n plus three sets of at most n entries
items.answer: O(n): recursion depth n plus three sets of at most n entries
items.explanation_md: Only one root-to-leaf path of the tree is live at any time, so the stack and the sets are linear in n. The tree itself is never stored.

items.prompt_md: Why is it fair to call constraint placement 'exponential but practical' for n = 8?
options: Early pruning removes most branches, so far fewer than 8! partial boards are actually explored
8 is smaller than the log of the input
The recursion is memoised
The algorithm switches to DP at depth 4
items.answer: Early pruning removes most branches, so far fewer than 8! partial boards are actually explored
items.explanation_md: Each unsafe candidate cuts away an entire subtree. The worst-case bound is still factorial, which is why interviews keep n small.

items.prompt_md: Each conflict check uses sets for columns and both diagonals. What does a single placement test cost?
options: O(n) to scan every placed queen
O(1) expected time, since it is three set membership tests
O(n^2) to rebuild the board
O(log n) with sorted lists
items.answer: O(1) expected time, since it is three set membership tests
items.explanation_md: Set membership replaces scanning previous queens, which would multiply the work by n at each node of the search.

items.prompt_md: Place 8 kings on a chessboard so that none attack each other, listing every valid placement, one per row.
options: Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Greedy choice
items.answer: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
items.explanation_md: One item per row with O(1) conflict tracking and pruning on conflict is constraint placement.

items.prompt_md: Fill the empty squares of a partially completed 9 x 9 number grid so each row, column and 3 x 3 box contains the digits 1 to 9 exactly once.
options: Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
items.answer: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
items.explanation_md: Choose a digit per empty cell, keep row/column/box sets, prune on conflict and undo. It is the same skeleton as N-Queens.

items.prompt_md: Count how many ways n towers can be placed on an n x n board such that no two share a column or either diagonal.
options: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
Greedy choice
items.answer: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
items.explanation_md: Counting solutions of a constraint puzzle still uses placement with pruning. There is no overlap-friendly state to DP over.

items.prompt_md: Find the largest total coin value from a grid by walking through four-direction moves without reusing a cell.
options: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
items.answer: Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
items.explanation_md: A route in a grid with cell reuse forbidden is grid backtracking. Conflict-set placement is about choosing one item per slot, not walking.

items.prompt_md: Generate every way to choose 3 numbers from 1 to 6.
options: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
Combinations: choose in increasing order
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.answer: Combinations: choose in increasing order
items.explanation_md: There is no conflict rule between chosen numbers, so no placement constraints. It is the combinations enumeration.

items.prompt_md: Given a list of tasks with deadlines and profits, pick tasks to maximise profit when each task takes one unit of time.
options: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
Dynamic programming over (row, col)
Greedy choice
items.answer: Greedy choice
items.explanation_md: A sorted greedy choice with a heap or slot structure works, not a search with conflict sets. Searching all placements would be exponential for no reason.

items.prompt_md: List every permutation of a small set of distinct numbers.
options: Permutations with a used-set
Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Subsets: include-or-skip recursion
Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
items.answer: Permutations with a used-set
items.explanation_md: No pair of placements conflicts except reuse of the same element, which a used-set handles. There is no diagonal-style rule, so this is the permutations pattern.

items.prompt_md: Find the minimum number of coins that sum to an amount, with unlimited coins of each denomination.
options: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Dynamic programming over amounts
Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
Permutations with a used-set
items.answer: Dynamic programming over amounts
items.explanation_md: Overlapping subproblems over the remaining amount mean a DP table. Searching every combination would repeat the same remaining amounts constantly.

items.prompt_md: Colour the regions of a small map using 4 colours so no two neighbouring regions share a colour, if possible.
options: Greedy choice
DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
BFS with a queue for the fewest steps
items.answer: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
items.explanation_md: Assign one colour per region, check conflicts with already coloured neighbours, prune and undo. A greedy order can get stuck and needs backtracking.

items.prompt_md: Count the connected groups of land in a grid.
options: Place one item per slot with conflict sets and pruning
Grid backtracking: mark, explore, unmark
Permutations with a used-set
DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
items.answer: DFS flood fill where cells stay visited
items.explanation_md: Each cell is visited once overall in a flood fill; there is no conflict rule to prune on.
